picks.who: Xunzi (Hsün Tzu, c. 310 to after 238 BCE)
picks.quote: ...a lame tortoise can go a thousand li by not resting a half step; by heaping up earth and not stopping, a mound or hill can be made high.
picks.work: Xunzi, Book II "Self-Cultivation" (Xiu Shen), section 21, in The Works of Hsüntze, tr. Homer H. Dubs (London: Arthur Probsthain, 1928), p. 50.
picks.meaning: A slow, hurt tortoise can still walk a very long way. It just never stops. Small steps every day add up.
picks.reason: I downloaded the OCR text of this archive.org scan (item in.ernet.dli.2015.103953; metadata says Dubs, Probsthain, 1928). It is Chapter II "Self-Cultivation", section 21, printed p. 50. The text reads: "For a lame tortoise can go a thousand li by not resting a half step ; by heaping up earth and not stopping, a mound or hill can be made high." The ellipsis stands in for the opening word "For", and every other word matches. The p. 51 ending is also confirmed: "...the lame tortoise arrives at the goal and the six noble steeds do not. There is no other reason for it than that the one keeps on and the other does not." So is the Book I alternate on p. 34: "A fast horse in one leap cannot go a thousand paces; but an old broken down nag can do it in ten days—its merit consists in not losing time." Dubs' footnote gives "a thousand li" as meaning a great distance. The SEP Xunzi entry backs up the dates (birth around 310 BCE, death after 238 BCE) and the phrase "the most revered of teachers". Xunzi is not on the used list; Confucius and Mencius are separate people. The excerpt has no rulers, war or religion in it. The meaning line is accurate, 21 words, with no long dash.

picks.who: Liezi (Lie Yukou, Daoist master, traditionally c. 400 BCE)
picks.quote: "Then you are not good enough yet," rejoined Kuan Yin Tzŭ. Lieh Tzŭ withdrew and practised for three years, after which he again presented himself.
picks.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, tr. Lionel Giles (London: John Murray, Wisdom of the East series, 1912), Book VII "Causality", p. 106 (original Liezi ch. 8, Shuo Fu).
picks.meaning: His teacher said, not good enough yet. He practiced three years and came back knowing why he hit the target.
picks.reason: I downloaded the OCR text of this archive.org scan (taoistteachings00liehuoft; Giles, John Murray, 1912; title page checked). In Book VII "Causality", printed p. 106, the text reads: "Then you are not good enough yet," rejoined Kuan Yin Tzu. Lieh Tzu withdrew and practised for three years, after which he again presented himself. The OCR drops the breve, and the printed form is Tzŭ. The story matches the summary: he could hit the target but did not know why, practised three years, then said "Yes, I do", and got the reply "Hold that knowledge fast, and do not let it slip." Giles' contents run I to VII, and his introduction says he left out the Yang Chu chapter, so Book VII is Liezi ch. 8 (Shuo Fu). Baidu Baike's entry on the story says Liezi learned archery from Guan Yin Zi, so "his teacher" holds up. Wikipedia puts Lie Yukou around the 5th century BCE, so "traditionally c. 400 BCE" is fine. Safety: the story is target practice only. Giles' own comment after the story mentions "the government of a State". That is not in the excerpt and should stay off the slide. The meaning line is accurate, 20 words, with no long dash.

picks.quote: Between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows... it is rough at the first; but when a man has reached the top, then is she easy to reach
picks.work: Works and Days, lines 286-292, translated by Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Loeb Classical Library, 1914 (Project Gutenberg eBook #348)
picks.meaning: The path is steep and hard at first. Keep sweating and climbing, and one day it feels easy.
picks.reason: I downloaded Gutenberg #348 (Evelyn-White, 1914) and found the passage under the heading (ll. 286-292), word for word: 'But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first; but when a man has reached the top, then is she easy to reach, though before that she was hard.' The ellipsis stands for 'long and steep is the path that leads to her, and', so every word in the excerpt is exact and in order. One small note: after that cut, 'it' has no clear subject, because the missing words said what 'it' was (the path). If there is room on the slide, add that clause back. The meaning line has no dates or events to check, is 18 words, uses plain English and has no long dash. The background facts are right: Hesiod lived around 700 BCE, came from Ascra in Boeotia and wrote the poem to his brother Perses (the text says 'foolish Perses'), and Plato and Xenophon quoted this passage. The backup line at ll. 361-362 ('add only a little to a little...') is also word for word in the same file. Content safety: the gods are named with respect and there is nothing about politics, war, royalty or disasters. Hesiod is not on the already-used list.

picks.quote: I had been a frail, irresolute, introverted child; by the time I reached manhood, I felt myself to be strong, vigorous and outgoing.
picks.work: Karate-Do: My Way of Life, Preface (Kodansha International, first English edition 1975; 1981 paperback, ISBN 0-87011-463-8; translator not credited)
picks.meaning: Funakoshi was born early and sickly in 1868. He trained karate at night for years, and in 1922 brought karate to Tokyo.
picks.reason: The quote matches word for word in the Preface of the koreankarate.com.au PDF. That PDF is an unofficial transcription, so I also checked the published book. An archive.org full-text search of the scanned Kodansha International paperback (item karatedomywayofl00funa, 1981, 'originally published c1975') returns the same words: 'I had been a frail, irresolute, introverted child; by the time I reached manhood, I felt myself to be strong, vigorous and outgoing.' No translator is named there. I checked the meaning line against the same text. 'Born prematurely, I was rather a sickly baby.' He gives 1868 as his birth year (official records say 1870, but Wikipedia uses 10 Nov 1868). Practice was 'held only at night', with nightly walks to Azato's house. 'Shortly after I came to Tokyo in 1922.' Wikipedia confirms the 1922 Kodokan demonstration. The meaning line is 22 words. It is safe: nothing on the government ban or the Imperial Palace. Funakoshi is not on the used list.

picks.who: Eugen Sandow, strongman and early physical-culture teacher
picks.quote: It is not necessary, as some may think, to be born strong in order to become strong. ... As a child, I was myself exceedingly delicate.
picks.work: Strength and How to Obtain It (revised edition, London: Gale & Polden, c. 1899; first published 1897), Part II 'Incidents of My Professional Career', Chapter I 'My Childhood and Boyhood', p. 85
picks.meaning: Sandow was a weak, sick boy until 18. He trained a little every day, and in 1889 he beat a famous strongman.
picks.reason: I downloaded Project Gutenberg eBook #65987 and matched the quote exactly. The ellipsis leaves out only 'Unlike the poet, who, we are told, has to be born a poet, the strong man can make himself.' The fix is to the citation. The part is headed 'PART II. INCIDENTS OF MY PROFESSIONAL CAREER', not 'Of My Professional Career', and Chapter I begins on p. 85. The title page says 'Revised Edition', Gale & Polden. Its pupil letters are dated 1899, which supports c. 1899. Wikipedia dates the first edition to 1897. I checked the meaning line against the book. 'More than once, indeed, my life was despaired of.' 'So until I was eighteen I remained delicate.' 'About fifteen minutes every day' of exercise. He beat Samson on '2nd of November, 1889'. Wikipedia confirms he was born 2 April 1867 and that in 1889 he 'beat the champion'. The meaning line is 22 words. It is safe: no Royal Aquarium, King George V or Army mentions. Sandow is not on the used list.

picks.quote: A small daily task, if it be really daily, will beat the labours of a spasmodic Hercules.
picks.work: An Autobiography (written 1875-76, published 1883 after his death), Chapter VII: "Doctor Thorne, The Bertrams, The West Indies and the Spanish Main". Project Gutenberg eBook #5978.
picks.meaning: Trollope was poor and friendless until 1841. Writing at 5:30 every morning, he finished 47 novels.
picks.reason: I downloaded the Gutenberg text (pg5978.txt). The quote appears word for word at line 3068, inside CHAPTER VII (starts line 3014). The passage matches: "...the water-drop that hollows the stone. A small daily task, if it be really daily, will beat the labours of a spasmodic Hercules. It is the tortoise which always catches the hare." Facts: Chapter VIII (line 3352) says "My life in England for twenty-six years... had been wretched. I had been poor, friendless, and joyless." In the autobiography he writes "On the 15th of September, 1841, I landed in Dublin", and Wikipedia also gives 1841 for the move to Ireland. Chapter XV (line 6677) says "It was my practice to be at my table every morning at 5.30 A.M." Wikipedia says "In all, Trollope wrote 47 novels". The meaning line is 16 words, has no long dash and is accurate. One small error in the context notes: "I hated the office. I hated my work." is at line 1448, which is Chapter III, not Chapter IV. Safety passes: the Hercules image stands for bursts of effort and does not mock him, and nothing touches politics or religion. He is not on the already-used list.

backups.quote: Whether young, old or too old, sick or lean, one who discards laziness, gets success if he practises Yoga.
backups.work: Hatha Yoga Pradipika, Chapter I (on Asanas), verse 66 in this edition (1.64 in the Bihar School/Muktibodhananda numbering), tr. Pancham Sinh (Allahabad: Sudhindra Nath Vasu, Panini Office, 1915; introduction dated Ajmer, 31 January 1915). Public domain.
backups.meaning: Young or old, sick or weak, anyone who stops being lazy and keeps practicing yoga will succeed.
backups.reason: I downloaded the OCR text of this archive.org scan (dli.csl.7087; Pancham Sinh). The English reads exactly: "Whether young, old or too old, sick or lean, one who discards laziness, gets success if he practises Yoga." It sits between verse 65 and "...one can never get success. 67.", so it is 66 in this edition. Verse 68 is also confirmed: "Practice alone is the means to... This is true, there is no doubt." Fix: this edition is dated 1915, not 1914. Sinh's introduction is signed "Ajmer: 31st January, 1915", archive.org metadata gives 1915, and the title page names Sudhindra Nath Vasu of the Panini Office, Allahabad, as publisher. Sacred-texts' "[1914]" cannot be squared with that date. The Muktibodhananda (Bihar School) text numbers the verse 64, so "1.64 in modern numberings" holds. Durbala does mean weak. The meaning line is accurate, 17 words, with no long dash. It is safe. Neither the person nor the line is on the used list, so it passes the letter of rule 4. Strong caution: this verse is the direct source of Pattabhi Jois' famous "anyone can practice... except lazy people". If the Jois slide already used is that saying, this repeats the same line and should be dropped. I could not find which Jois line was used.

backups.quote: ...I’ll get back to drawing... and now I’m on my way and my pencil has become somewhat obedient and seems to become more so day by day.
backups.work: Letter 158 to Theo van Gogh, Cuesmes, Friday 24 September 1880. English translation from Vincent van Gogh: The Letters (eds. Leo Jansen, Hans Luijten, Nienke Bakker; Van Gogh Museum and Huygens ING, 2009), vangoghletters.org.
backups.meaning: In 1880 Van Gogh was broke and slept outdoors. He drew daily; in ten years he made over 800 paintings.
backups.reason: I fetched letter 158 from vangoghletters.org. The header reads "To Theo van Gogh. Cuesmes, Friday, 24 September 1880". The full sentence is on the page: "...I’ll pick up my pencil that I put down in my great discouragement and I’ll get back to drawing, and from then on, it seems to me, everything has changed for me, and now I’m on my way and my pencil has become somewhat obedient and seems to become more so day by day." The ellipses only leave out words and do not change the meaning. Facts: the same letter says he was in "extreme poverty" and that when "my ten francs were gone, I had to bivouac out in the open for the last 3 nights" (an abandoned carriage, a wood-pile, a haystack). So "broke and slept outdoors" is true, though it was 3 nights on a walking trip. Wikipedia says "In just over a decade he created about 2,100 artworks, including around 860 oil paintings", so "over 800 paintings" in "ten years" is correct. The meaning line is 20 words and has no long dash. Safety passes: nothing is said about his illness or how his life ended, so keep it that way on the card. He is not on the already-used list.

backups.quote: ...the habit of energetic industry and of concentrated attention to whatever I was engaged in... I feel sure that it was this training which has enabled me to do whatever I have done in science.
backups.work: The Autobiography of Charles Darwin (written 1876; ed. Francis Darwin, published in Life and Letters, 1887), section "Voyage of the 'Beagle' from December 27, 1831, to October 2, 1836". Project Gutenberg eBook #2010.
backups.meaning: Darwin's teachers thought him 'a very ordinary boy.' Daily focus on a five-year sea voyage from 1831 made him a great scientist.
backups.reason: I downloaded the Gutenberg text (pg2010.txt). The source reads: "...the habit of energetic industry and of concentrated attention to whatever I was engaged in, which I then acquired. Everything about which I thought or read was made to bear directly on what I had seen... during the five years of the voyage. I feel sure that it was this training which has enabled me to do whatever I have done in science." It is in the section headed "VOYAGE OF THE 'BEAGLE' FROM DECEMBER 27, 1831, TO OCTOBER 2, 1836" (line 891). The ellipses are honest: "this training" refers back to the same habit. Facts: the book says "I was considered by all my masters and by my father as a very ordinary boy, rather below the common standard in intellect." The voyage began on 27 Dec 1831, and Darwin himself calls it "the five years of the voyage". "Made him a great scientist" is a fair plain-English version of his own claim that the training enabled all he did in science. The meaning line is exactly 22 words, has no long dash, and uses a single-quoted phrase. Safety passes: the quote and meaning say nothing about evolution or religion, and the voyage is described only as a "sea voyage". Keep the card off the Origin/evolution debate and do not use the Galton letter line, as the notes already advise. He is not on the already-used list.

backups.who: Annette Kellerman (spelled Kellermann in the book), Australian champion swimmer
backups.quote: My brothers and sister had learned to swim in four or five lessons, but eighteen were required for me. ... little by little I found that my legs were growing stronger...
backups.work: How to Swim (New York: George H. Doran Company, 1918), Part I 'The Story of My Swim to Fame and Fortune', Chapter I 'The Little Girl Who Was Afraid of the Water', pp. 14-15
backups.meaning: Annette wore steel leg braces as a small child. Swimming slowly made her legs strong, and by 1902 she was a champion.
backups.reason: I pulled the archive.org OCR text of the 1918 Doran scan. The original reads: 'My brothers and sister had learned to swim in four or five lessons, but eight-een were required for me. Only a cripple can understand the intense joy [p.15] that I experienced when little by little I found that my legs were growing stronger and taking on the normal shape...' The cut is fair and keeps the meaning. The only fix is a trailing ellipsis, because the sentence goes on after 'stronger'. The part, chapter titles and pages 14-15 all match the contents page and running heads. The steel braces are in the same chapter ('painful and humiliating steel braces'). Wikipedia says she wore braces from age six and won the 1902 NSW 100 yards and mile titles in record times. The meaning line is 22 words. It is safe, and she is not on the used list.
